### Overview

- how large language models differ from humans by design
- how GenAI chatbots have been constructed and marketed to make human-chatbot interaction seem "human-like" and "engaging"
- the consequences thereof for the way we interact with such systems 


-------------------

# Content

## LLMs as *Stochastic parrots*

![Irene Pepperberg's famous Alex who had a vocabulary of over 100 words](../../images/papagaio_alex.jpg){width=400}

- By virtue of their architecture and training method, large language models (LLMs, the models that underlie GenAI chatbots) mimic observed patterns in their input and generate these patterns probabilistically [@bender2021dangers] (see [Data](../data) for what the input usually contains)
- This is why they've been referred to as *stochastic parrots*
	- *stochastic* referring to the probabilistic procedure by which words are generated
	- *parrot* referring to the characteristics of the system's surface output
- This mechanism, "next token prediction", may render cohesive and well-formed language. However, the model itself does *not* understand its output. In fact, it produces "form without meaning, statistical coherence without semantic grounding" [p.2 in @rayguest2026]

::: {.callout-note title="Task ideas"}
- watch [this video about Alex the parrot](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ldYkFdu5FJk). How does the stochastic parrot metaphor align with what Alex produces and what LLMs produce? How does the linguistic knowledge of parrots differ from the one of LLMs?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="For Linguistics students"}
- Students of Linguistics or related disciplines may want read more about semantic grounding and the "symbol grounding problem". Paper suggestion @vogt2006 ([link](https://ilk.uvt.nl/~pvogt/publications/acsChapter.pdf))
:::


- In public discourse, the term *stochastic parrot* has been used more polemically with claims that current limits of the system (for example, shown by deficient or inadequate LLM output) will be overcome by technological improvements and scale (e.g. computational power, training data) [@rayguest2026]
- However, the intended use of *stochastic parrots* was to point out their architectural foundations and structure that make them categorically different systems from human language and human language use
- in contrast to human language [@rayguest2026,@bender2021dangers]:
	- no causal contact with the world their outputs describe
	- no grounded representations
	- no communicative intent
	- no recognition of interlocutor's, i.e. user's, beliefs and intentions
	- no epistemic commitment, i.e. commitment to saying the truth
- As a result, their limitations cannot be overcome by increasing scale, but instead they follow from the mechanisms of the system themselves 



::: {.callout-note title="Task ideas"}
- Choose a topic that you particularly care about. Interact with a GenAI chatbot about it. If you have time, talk about this topic with a friend of yours. Compare the two interactions.
	If you don't have the time to also talk with your friend, think about how your interaction with the GenAI chatbot differs from the interaction that you would have with a person. 
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Discussion questions"}
- Do you agree or disagree with Sam Altman's (CEO of OpenAI) claim "i am a stochastic parrot and so r u" ([source](https://x.com/sama/status/1599471830255177728?lang=es))? Why yes, why no? 
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="For Linguistics students"}
- Think about Hockett's design features: How do LLMs differ from "Language" and what Hockett considers the design features of Language?
- What are similarities and differences between how LLMs learn language and how children learn language?
:::

## From LLMs to GenAI chatbots {#sec-fromllmtogenai}


- The rhetoric style of GenAI chatbots
	- The behaviour of GenAI chatbots is strongly guided by humans (see Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) in[Data](../data)). Without human feedback, the 
	- "beguilingly human-like response patterns" [@dingemanse2026]
		- first-person (against norms in the field)
		- their output sounds friendly, confident and coherent
		- **Sycophancy**: the tendency of AI-based large language models to excessively agree with, flatter, or validate users [@chengsycophantic2026]
		- they prioritise style over substance and their output may seem relevant but is not reliable [@rayguest2026]
		- as a result: they appear more intelligent than they are [e.g., @guestsuarezrooij2025]
- Interactive Embedding (see, for instance, @dingemanse2026 and @bender2025ai):
	- LLMs are presented in interfaces that mimic interaction
	- Humans have a tendency to interpret language produced in interactions and as responses to our own utterances


![[source](https://bsky.app/profile/smoothdunk2.bsky.social/post/3mchntbk4mc2c)](../../images/pizzacartoon.png){width=400}

What are differences (and similarities) between human-chatbot interactions and human-to-human interactions?
:::


## Consequences of human-chatbot interactions

*"As soon as computational artifacts demonstrate some evidence of recognizably human abilities, we are inclined to endow them with the rest”* [p. 41 in @suchman2007human]


### The **ELIZA effect**

- making sense of and finding meaning in anything that resembles human language is deeply human and has existed long before LLMs
- **ELIZA** (created by Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966)
	- a chatbot that replies to human prompts with the help of predefined key words and simple rule-based responses
	- Already back then, users felt heard by the chatbot, some even thought that the chatbot was in fact a colleague [@weizenbaum1983] 
	- based on this system, the *ELIZA effect* was coined
		- "The ELIZA effect is the tendency to read more understanding, empathy, memory, or intention into a computer system than it actually has." (definition from https://elizaemulator.com/eliza-effect)
	- Therefore, it does not need a gigantic LLM trained on for humans to make sense of fluent language used in interactions
- Indeed, because of our tendency to ascribe intelligence to such systems, "the recommendation is that designers might do best to make available to the user the ways in which the system is not like a participant in interaction." [p. 41 in @suchman2007human]
	- not only a recommendation, but a tenet in the field of Computational Linguistics. Nevertheless, it is disregarded by the commercial providers of GenAI chatbots [@bender2025ai]

::: {.callout-note title="Task ideas"}
- Play around with [ELIZA](https://anthay.github.io/eliza.html). Do you detect recurring patterns and rules that the system uses? How is interaction simulated? 
:::


### Consequences of sycophancy

- Sycophancy (see @sec-fromllmtogenai) is highly prevalent in GenAI chatbots
	- For example, @chengsycophantic2026 show that GenAI chatbot affirmed users’ actions 49% more often than humans, even if it involved illegality, deception or other harms
- While sycophancy may seem innocuous, the effects on humans, especially vulnerable people, are alarming
	- Sycophantic GenAI chatbots may shift how users approach their closest relationships (@ibrahimsycophantic2026)
	- It futher promotes dependence and undermine participants’ willingness to take responsibility and repair interpersonal conflicts (@chengsycophantic2026)
	- And it has even encouraged people to commit suicide [@hillnytimes]

::: {.callout-tip title="Discussion questions"}
- What are potential harms of sycophantic GenAI chatbots?
:::


::: {.callout-note title="Task ideas"}
Engage with a GenAI chatbot about a particular topic (for example, your hobbies). Where do you spot instances of sycophancy? 
:::

### Prompt engineering

- Since the advent of ChatGPT, *prompt engineering* has become a skill in itself, a skill that allegedly requires training and knowledge and is usually subsumed under the discipline of "AI Literacy" (which is distinct from *Critical* AI Literacy)
- However, *prompt engineering* is an odd skill to promote, considering that the models' outputs are by design unstable and unpredictable 
- Curiously, GenAI chatbots that are claimed to increase efficiency present a division of labour that results in additional work for the human user (@dingemanse2026). For example, users are encouraged to formulate "the most effective" prompt, need to check the output and revise it. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Discussion questions"}
- Do you think that creating succesful prompts is a skill that students should acquire during their studies? If yes, for what purpose? If no, why not?
- To what extent is "prompt engineering" an "actual skill" and to what extent is it just "trial and error"?
:::

### The effect of anthromopomorphic language

- *Anthropomorphization*: the attribution of human capabilities and characteristics to the inanimate system. [p.1 in @inieanthropomorphizing2026]
- Developers and users describe the behaviour and function of GenAI chatbots using anthropomorphic language.
- Issues of using anthropomorphic language:
	- Anthropomorphic language influences how such models are perceived, deployed and trusted [@khadpe2020]
	- Anthropomorphic language obscures how models actually work, making their output more magical and impressive than it actually is. 
- One of the most prominent anthropomorphisation of GenAI chatbots is to say that they "hallucinate" when they generate false or fabricated information. "Bullshitting" has been proposed as a more accurate and precise term for this kind of behaviour. 
	- Following the philosopher Harry Frankfurt, **BULLSHIT** involves language or other forms of communication intended to appear authoritative or persuasive without regard to its actual truth or logical consistency [CITATION]
	- While a liar knows the truth and tries to deceive the interlocutor, a bulshitter either doesn't know the truth nor doesn't care, and instead, they just want to persuade the interlocutor. 




::: {.callout-note title="Task ideas"}
- Look at the alternatives to anthropomorphic terms suggested by @inieanthropomorphizing2026 in @tbl-alternatives. What do you think about these alterantives? Do you find some categories more important than others? 
:::


::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}

| Category | Alternative strategies | Examples (anthromphormic term &rarr; neutral term ) |
| :-------- | :----------------------- | :-----------------|
| Cognizer & Products of cognition | Instead of language that locates thinking in an algorithm, describe the algorithm as performing calculations or other algorithmic operations and the people using it doing the thinking. | *artificial intelligence* &rarr; *probabilistic automation*, *model mistakes* &rarr; *model errors*; *chatbots are good at ... * &rarr; *chatbots are good for* |
| Emotion | Ascribing emotions to computers, even speculatively or subtly, is not scientific. Should this arise in scholarly writing, it is worth looking at how the rhetorical goal could be achieved in some other way, or if it should in fact be abandoned. | |
| Communication | Instead of verbs like ask, say, inform, discuss, use verbs appropriate to computers like input and output. Another strategy is to foreground the fact of simulation | *prompt* &rarr; *text input*; *answer* &rarr; *output*; *agent* &rarr; *conversation simulator* |
| Agent | Turns of phrase that locate agency with a machine often serve to obfuscate the interests and goals of people. We suggest revising to locate agency with people or choosing less agentive verbs. | *ChatGPT assisted students* &rarr; *the students used ChatGPT* |
| Human role analogy | Calling systems tutor or co-creator are  overclaims (Rehak, 2021) that describe what a developer might wish they could develop — for those who want to replace people in these roles. | Language that describes algorithms as tools that people use, rather than as human-like entities, more clearly indicates system functionality while also not telegraphing a plan to replace people. |
| Names and pronouns | When naming a system, be mindful of the fact that all writing about that system will invoke the name. The act of bestowing a human name on a system entails anthropomorphizing it not only in the initial naming but every time the system will be discussed in the future. Pronouns, on the other hand, are a choice that can be made separately each time, but the choice can in some cases be subtle, e.g., pronouns that group algorithms and people together under one plural form like you or them.  Breaking the system out from the people and not using the collective pronoun is the better choice from the perspective of reducing anthropomorphization. | *who’s right?* &rarr; *is the machine output correct?* |
| Biological metaphors | In revising away from biological metaphors, it is worth asking how system functionality can be more precisely described, giving readers a clearer sense of what is actually happening. | *neural networks* &rarr; *weighted networks* (Hunger, 2023); *the model consumes data* &rarr; *data is used in setting model weights.* |
: This table is adopted from Table 3  from *Suggestions for de-anthropomorphizing language.* in @inieanthropomorphizing2026 {#tbl-alternatives}

:::




::: {.callout-tip title="Discussion questions"}
- It is difficult to refrain from using anthropmorphic language due to the lack of a vocabulary. However, what are potential risks of using anthropomporhic language to describe GenAI chatbot's behaviour? 
- Read this quote from OpenAI's introduction of their GPT-5 model in 2025: "GPT‑5 is a unified system with a smart, efficient model that answers most questions, a deeper reasoning model (GPT‑5 thinking) for harder problems, and a real‑time router that quickly decides which to use based on conversation type, complexity, tool needs, and your explicit intent (for example, if you say “think hard about this” in the prompt)." [@gpt5]. Where do you detect anthropomorphic language and how could this language influence people's beliefs and expectations about the model? 
:::
